title: The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation: building micrograd
note: SYNTHETIC SAMPLE: paraphrased summary of themes from this video, written for offline testing. NOT a verbatim transcript. Run `./run.sh ingest <playlist>` locally to fetch the real one.

segments.text: Today we are going to build a tiny autograd engine from scratch so you really understand what is happening under the hood.
My philosophy is that you should be able to build it yourself; if you can write it from scratch in a hundred lines you actually understand it.
Start with the simplest possible thing that works end to end, a single scalar value object, and only then add complexity.
We will make a Value class that stores data and a gradient, and records the operation that produced it.
Always visualize what you are building; I draw the computation graph so I can see every node and every gradient.
Check your gradients numerically. Nudge the input by a tiny h and compare against the analytic derivative; this catches a lot of bugs.
A very common bug is forgetting to accumulate gradients with plus equals; if a variable is used twice the gradient gets overwritten.
Another classic bug: forgetting to zero the gradients before the backward pass. Your loss looks like it is training but it is wrong.
When something goes wrong, do not stare at the code; print the intermediate values, look at the actual numbers, form a hypothesis.
Write a tiny test that compares your engine against PyTorch on the same expression; if both agree you can trust it.
Keep the code small and readable. Simplicity is a feature, especially when you need to debug it at two in the morning.
Get a working training loop first: forward pass, compute loss, backward, update. Then iterate on the model.
Do not optimize prematurely. A slow correct implementation beats a fast wrong one every single time.
The learning rate is the first thing I tune. If the loss explodes the learning rate is too high; if it barely moves it is too low.
Overfit a single tiny batch first. If you cannot drive the loss to near zero on four examples, something is broken.
Build intuition by playing with it interactively in a notebook; change one thing at a time and watch what happens.
Things I warn against: copying large frameworks you do not understand, and adding features before the core loop works.
Once the core works, wrapping it into a neat library with neurons, layers and an MLP is just a small amount of organization.
